recent_posts.title: Building a neural network in four languages from PyTorch to Scratch
recent_posts.summary: A developer builds the same neural network for handwritten digit recognition (0s and 1s) in four progressively difficult implementations: PyTorch, NumPy, pure C, and finally Scratch (the visual programming language). The journey demonstrates fundamental ML concepts like forward/backward passes, loss functions, and gradient descent, starting with high-level abstractions and ending with manual matrix operations using logic blocks. The Scratch implementation required downsizing images from 28x28 to 10x10 pixels and reducing hidden layer neurons to 10, but successfully trains and classifies digits.

recent_posts.title: Building an AI to speedrun Wikipedia using embeddings and LLMs
recent_posts.summary: A developer built an AI system to speedrun Wikipedia by navigating from one article to another using only internal links. The project explores two approaches: a BERT-based embedding model that calculates vector distances to find optimal paths, and large language models (Gemini Flash, Claude) that leverage their training data. Performance testing across 3,000 random Wikipedia challenges showed LLMs completing tasks in 12-30 seconds with fewer clicks (3.6 average) compared to the embedding approach (43 links average). A human vs AI competition revealed humans averaged 2 minutes 16 seconds and 4.3 clicks, demonstrating AI's significant advantage in this navigation task.

recent_posts.title: Building a tennis prediction model that outperformed IBM at Wimbledon
recent_posts.summary: A developer improves their tennis match prediction model by implementing proper machine learning practices including training/validation/test set splits, hyperparameter tuning, and systematic experimentation. The refined model achieved 75% accuracy predicting Wimbledon Round 3 matches, outperforming IBM's 56% accuracy.

recent_posts.title: Building an AI tennis prediction model for Wimbledon
recent_posts.summary: A developer continues their AI-powered tennis prediction experiment for Wimbledon's second round, improving their XGBoost model's accuracy from 61% to 62.5% by incorporating additional player data. The main challenge was missing data for qualifier players, which limited prediction accuracy for matches involving lesser-known competitors. Despite the improvement, IBM's competing model achieved 68.8% accuracy.

recent_posts.title: Building an XGBoost model to predict Wimbledon tennis matches
recent_posts.summary: A developer rebuilds their tennis match prediction model using XGBoost after discovering data leakage issues in their previous attempt. After scraping 40,000 tennis matches and training the model, they achieved 61% accuracy on Wimbledon's first round predictions, outperforming IBM's 55% accuracy despite various challenges including unexpected upsets and extreme weather conditions.

recent_posts.title: Building massive Sudoku puzzles with recursive backtracking algorithms
recent_posts.summary: A developer creates increasingly complex Sudoku puzzles using recursive backtracking algorithms, starting with solving 10 million puzzles in under 2 minutes with C++, then building the world's longest Sudoku with 500 connected puzzles, and finally creating a massive 20,000x20,000 pixel puzzle containing 4,810 interconnected hard-rated Sudokus. The project demonstrates algorithm implementation, performance optimization between Python and C++, and puzzle generation techniques.

recent_posts.title: I Coded a 3D Spinning Donut
recent_posts.summary: A developer recreates the famous spinning ASCII donut from scratch using C++, explaining the mathematical concepts behind 3D graphics rendering in terminals. The journey covers rotation matrices, 3D to 2D projection, lighting calculations, and extends to creating ASCII cubes and pyramids. The tutorial breaks down complex linear algebra concepts into digestible explanations while documenting debugging challenges and creative variations like colored donuts with sprinkles.

recent_posts.title: How prime numbers became illegal through DVD encryption
recent_posts.summary: Explores the concept of illegal prime numbers, specifically focusing on how certain prime numbers can be used to decrypt DVD copyright protection, making them legally restricted. Demonstrates a C++ implementation that calculated over 130 million prime numbers in one minute, reaching prime number 2,782,486,301.
